Great to meet you and Tom today — thanks for walking us through your ingestion flow and the SLA needs. Per our call, I wanted to recap next steps and surface one area you asked us to clarify: how to handle rate limiting / 429s + retries for your synchronous inference endpoints and embedding/reranker workflows.

Quick summary of next steps:
- Ben: Send integration guide and short summary of SDK auth & routing patterns (attached).
- Marissa: Follow up with concrete retry/idempotency recommendations and sample request header patterns.
- Vivek: Confirm expected throughput for the POC (you mentioned ~200 req/s peak for reranks).
- ACME: Share expected query/embedding cardinality and retention window.

I've attached the Redwood SDK integration guide and a brief note on rate-limits. Below are the main points we covered and the items Marissa will expand on in her note.

High-level behavior we recommend:
- Client-side rate limiting + token-bucket smoothing to avoid bursty 429s.
- Respect Retry-After when returned; use exponential backoff + jitter for retries.
- Use idempotency keys for state-changing calls; use request IDs for observability & dedupe.
- For embeddings + rerank: prefilter candidates with light-weight signals (caching, lexical filters) to reduce calls, and batch/embed async where possible.

Attachments: redwood-sdk-integration-guide.pdf, acme-rate-limits-summary.pdf

Thanks — will loop Marissa in for the detailed tech note.

Subject: Re: Follow-up: Integration & Rate-limits (post-demo)

Elena — thanks for the questions. Below is a concrete set of recommendations we use with customers in similar POC shapes. I kept it pragmatic so your infra folks can implement quickly.

1) Retry semantics & idempotency (user-facing sync endpoints)
- Idempotency: For any call that can cause a side effect (writes, billing events), include an Idempotency-Key header (UUIDv4) and persist it server-side for a TTL slightly longer than the client retry window (e.g., 10–60 minutes depending on your flow). Redwood will return the same result for identical idempotency keys when applicable.
- Request IDs: Always send X-Request-ID (UUID) per logical operation — useful to tie client logs, redwood logs, and billing traces. We also echo back X-Request-ID in responses for easier correlation.
- Retry strategy: Use an exponential backoff with full jitter. Example: base=200ms, factor=2, max_delay=10s, max_retries=4. If server returns Retry-After (seconds), respect it as a minimum before the next attempt.
- Safe retries: Design your client to treat POSTs as potentially non-idempotent unless you send an Idempotency-Key. For synchronous product flows, we recommend generating an idempotency key at the user-action boundary (e.g., per submit button click).

2) Rate limiting & quotas
- Client-side throttling: Token-bucket or leaky-bucket smoothing is effective to avoid bursts (we can share a small library sample). Configure per-route limits (e.g., separate buckets for /v1/generate vs /v1/embeddings).
- Server-side signals: Redwood returns 429 with a Retry-After header when you hit quotas. We recommend tracking 429 rate and setting alerts (e.g., >0.5% of requests 429 for 5m).
- Backpressure: For user-facing requests, surface a graceful degrade (retry with backoff once, then show a friendly rate-limit UI). For background batch jobs, prefer queueing + async processing to avoid sync retries.

3) Partial failures & batching (embeddings + rerank)
- Batch semantics: If you batch M items into a single embeddings call, the SDK returns a list of results. We recommend designing for partial failures: identify per-item status and retry only failed items instead of reshuffling the entire batch.
- Reranker pattern: Candidate generation -> embeddings prefilter -> rerank call. Aim to keep reranker calls smaller and use embedding vectors + cheap heuristics to reduce the number of rerank inputs (cache top-K embeddings per query when possible).
- SDK helpers: Our SDK includes batch helpers and per-item error metadata (index-level errors). It will return an array where each position maps to an input; errors include canonical error codes and the original index so you can selectively retry.

4) Headers & telemetry
- Recommended headers to include on every call:
  - Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY> (or mTLS token for Private installs)
  - X-Request-ID: <uuid> (logical op-level)
  - Idempotency-Key: <uuid> (for mutating ops)
  - X-Client-Version: acme-search-service/1.2.0
  - X-Route-Hint: "{\"model\":\"redwood-7b\", \"latency_budget_ms\":200}" (optional JSON string)

5) Operational knobs we can provide for the POC
- Per-customer rate limits and adjustable quotas for the POC window.
- Canary routing: route a small % of traffic to a cheaper/quantized variant and fall back on 429 or higher latency.
- Request-level fallbacks: streaming -> non-streaming fallback; model fallback when latency SLOs are missed.

6) Implementation snippet (pseudocode)

Client-side (pseudocode):
  function callModel(request) {
    const id = uuid(); // x-request-id
    const idem = uuid(); // idempotency-key for user action if needed
    tryWithBackoff(() => http.post('/v1/generate', request, headers={Authorization, 'X-Request-ID': id, 'Idempotency-Key': idem}), maxRetries=4);
  }

Backoff logic: use exponential backoff with full jitter
  - attemptDelay = random_between(0, base * (2 ** attempt))
  - cap delay to max_delay and respect Retry-After if provided

7) Monitoring / SLOs
- Track request count, 429 count, Retry-After occurrences, p95 latency per route, and client-side retry counts.
- Add a dashboard that ties X-Request-ID to Redwood traces and response sizes.

If helpful, I can attach a small Node/Go client example and a short token-bucket snippet you can drop into your gateway. Vivek — if you can confirm expected QPS per route (embeddings vs rerank vs gen) we can pre-configure a POC quota and TTL for idempotency caching.

Thanks,
Marissa
